approachQuestion.prompt:
Minimum swaps to order IDs

The input is an array of distinct signed 32-bit integers. One operation swaps any two positions. Return the minimum number of swaps needed to place all values in ascending order. 1≤n≤200000. Examples: [40,10,30]→2; [2,1]→1.

Do not modify either input. Values are opaque comparison keys; hashing, radix, counting and bucket methods are outside the stated model. Choose the most efficient valid method that returns the required result for every allowed input.
constraints: Inputs are read-only and must remain unchanged.
Only comparison-based ordering is allowed; hashing, radix, counting and bucket methods are outside this problem model.

options.text: Sort (value, originalIndex) records by value ascending to derive each original index’s destination position; traverse that permutation’s cycles with a visited array and sum L−1 for each cycle of length L.
options.feedback: Sorting defines the destination mapping for arbitrary distinct values. Each cycle of positions needs exactly L−1 unrestricted swaps, and cycle costs add independently.

options.text: Count adjacent swaps needed to sort the array.
options.feedback: Adjacent swaps are not the allowed-cost objective. For [3,2,1], adjacent swaps need 3, while one swap of the endpoints sorts the array.

options.text: Count values that are not already in their final ascending position.
options.feedback: Every element in [2,3,1] is displaced, so this returns 3, but swapping indices 0 and 2 gives [1,3,2], then swapping indices 1 and 2 sorts it: only 2 swaps.

options.text: Sort a copy, count positions differing from the input, and return half that count rounded upward.
options.feedback: Not every swap can settle two positions. For [2,3,4,1], this returns 2, but its single cycle of length four requires 3 swaps.

feedback.reason: A permutation cycle of length L needs L-1 swaps: each swap can place another member correctly.
details: Copy values into (value, originalIndex) records and sort by value ascending. This defines a destination-position permutation for the original indices. Traverse each cycle once with a visited array; a cycle of length L contributes L−1 swaps.

A permutation cycle of length L needs L-1 swaps: each swap can place another member correctly. Mark each cycle once to avoid charging it from every node. Distinct IDs make destination positions unambiguous.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed below, choose the tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds. Count the indexed working copy, merge-sort buffer and visited array; exclude input and the scalar result. Comparisons, arithmetic, record copies and array accesses take constant time; merge sort uses a linear buffer.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort indexed IDs, then traverse disjoint permutation cycles once.
details: Sorting n indexed values through logarithmic merge levels costs O(n log n). Disjoint-cycle traversal adds O(n) because every original index is marked once. Indexed records, merge buffer, and visited flags are all linear auxiliary arrays, even though the result is only a swap count.
